entry: Membrane-bound organelle of [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic]] cells, containing nearly all of the cell's genome. Most eukaryotic cells have a single nucleus, though mammalian [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]] have none and some cell types have many. The nuclear envelope, a double membrane, separates the nucleus's contents from the [[Cytoplasm|cytoplasm]], and a network called the nuclear matrix adds mechanical support. Nuclear [[DNA]] is organized into [[Chromosome|chromosomes]] with proteins such as histones, and the nucleus regulates [[Gene expression|gene expression]] and the activities of the cell. Nuclear pores control the passage of molecules across the envelope; larger molecules such as proteins and [[RNA]] must be actively transported through them. The nucleolus, the best-known of the nuclear bodies, is involved in assembling [[Ribosome|ribosomes]].

Biological process by which cells interact with themselves, with other cells and with their environment. Signals are mostly chemical molecules that bind and activate a specific receptor, such as [[Ion|ions]], [[Lipid|lipids]] and [[Peptide|peptides]], though physical cues such as pressure, voltage, temperature and light also serve. Signaling typically involves three components: the first messenger (the ligand), the receptor and the signal itself. Cell membrane receptors include ion channel-linked, G-protein coupled and enzyme-linked types, while intracellular receptors bind lipid-soluble ligands, such as steroid hormones, that pass through the [[Cell membrane|plasma membrane]]. Signaling is classed as autocrine (acting on the same cell), juxtacrine (between adjacent cells), paracrine (between nearby cells) or endocrine (between distant cells, with the [[Hormone|hormone]] usually carried by the blood). Second messenger systems can amplify a signal, and errors in signaling may cause [[Cancer|cancer]], autoimmunity and [[Diabetes|diabetes]].

Structural layer outside the cell membrane of many cell types. The cell wall can be tough, flexible or rigid, and gives the cell support, shape and protection. It acts as a selective barrier and helps the cell withstand osmotic pressure and mechanical stress. Cell walls are found in most [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]], except mollicute bacteria, and in fungi, [[Algae|algae]] and [[Plant|plants]], but are absent from animals. Composition varies: the primary cell wall of land plants is made of polysaccharides such as [[Cellulose|cellulose]], hemicelluloses and pectin; bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan; fungal walls are built from [[Chitin|chitin]]; and [[Diatom|diatoms]] have walls of biogenic silica. [[Robert Hooke]] first observed and named the plant cell wall in 1665.

Medium-low-pitched bowed string instrument of the [[Violin|violin]] family. Its four strings are usually tuned in perfect fifths, from low to high: C2, G2, D3 and A3. Music for the cello is generally written in bass clef, with tenor and treble clefs for higher passages. It has a large solo repertoire and numerous concertos. In [[Chamber music|chamber music]] and the orchestral string section it usually plays the bass or tenor part, often reinforced an octave lower by [[Double bass|double basses]]. In [[Baroque|Baroque]] music it was typically part of the basso continuo, alongside chordal instruments such as the organ, [[Harpsichord|harpsichord]] and [[Lute|lute]]. Originating in northern Italy in the early 16th century, it was refined in the late 17th and early 18th centuries by makers including [[Antonio Stradivari]] and the Guarneri family.

Process by which cells oxidize fuels such as [[Sugar|sugars]], [[Amino acid|amino acids]] and [[Fatty acid|fatty acids]] to produce [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] (ATP), which stores chemical energy in a usable form. An electron acceptor receives the electrons in the process, most commonly molecular [[Oxygen|oxygen]]. When oxygen is the acceptor it is called aerobic respiration; when another molecule is used it is anaerobic. [[Fermentation|Fermentation]], also anaerobic, transfers electrons to organic molecules and is not classed as respiration. Although technically a combustion reaction, respiration releases energy slowly and in controlled steps, some of them redox reactions. Aerobic respiration unfolds in four main stages: [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]], pyruvate oxidation, the [[Citric acid cycle|citric acid cycle]] and oxidative phosphorylation via the electron transport chain.

Polysaccharide of linear chains of several hundred to many thousands of β(1→4)-linked [[Glucose|D-glucose]] units, with the formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ. It is the most abundant organic polymer on Earth and a major structural component of the [[Cell wall|cell walls]] of green plants, many [[Algae|algae]], [[Oomycete|oomycetes]] and sea squirts. Some [[Bacteria|bacteria]] secrete it to form biofilms. The cellulose content is 90% for cotton fiber, 40–50% for wood and approximately 57% for dried hemp. Industrially it is obtained mainly from wood pulp and cotton and is used chiefly for [[Paper|paper]] and paperboard, with smaller amounts converted into products such as cellophane and [[Rayon|rayon]]. [[Termite|Termites]] and ruminants digest it with the help of gut microbes, and in humans it is a non-digestible part of dietary fiber.

Unit of temperature on the scale originally called centigrade, one of the two temperature scales of the [[International System of Units|International System of Units]] (SI), the other being the [[Kelvin|kelvin]] scale. The degree (°C) can denote a specific point on the scale or a difference between two temperatures. The scale is named after Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius, who proposed a first version in 1742. The International Committee for Weights and Measures renamed the unit in 1948 to honor him. For much of the 19th and 20th centuries the scale was based on 0 °C for the freezing point of water and 100 °C for its boiling point at 1 atm, although Celsius's initial proposal reversed these values. Since 2007 the scale has been defined in terms of the kelvin, with absolute zero exactly 0 K, or −273.15 °C. Most countries use the scale; the United States and some island territories use [[Fahrenheit|Fahrenheit]].

Collection of Indo-European peoples in Europe and Anatolia who shared Celtic languages and cultural traits. Major groups included the [[Gaul|Gauls]], the Celtiberians and Gallaeci of [[Iberian Peninsula|Iberia]], the Britons, Picts and Gaels of Britain and Ireland, the Boii and the Galatians. In current scholarship the term primarily refers to speakers of Celtic languages rather than to a single ethnic group. Theories of origin place proto-Celtic in central Europe, the Atlantic coast or Gaul. The [[Iron Age|Iron Age]] Hallstatt culture (c. 1200–500 BC) and the La Tène culture (c. 450 BC onward) are associated with its spread, which reached central [[Anatolia|Anatolia]] after the Celtic settlement of Southeast Europe in the 3rd century BC. The earliest undisputed Celtic inscriptions, in Lepontic, date from the 6th century BC. [[Roman Empire|Roman expansion]] absorbed most continental Celtic groups, while insular Celts in Ireland and parts of Britain resisted longer.

Binder used in construction that sets, hardens and adheres to other materials. Cement is seldom used alone; mixed with fine aggregate it makes mortar for masonry, and mixed with [[Sand|sand]] and [[Gravel|gravel]] it makes [[Concrete|concrete]], the most widely used material in existence, behind only water as the planet's most-consumed resource. Hydraulic cements such as Portland cement set through a chemical reaction with water, allowing them to harden underwater, while non-hydraulic cements set as they dry by reacting with [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] in the air. Ancient Romans developed the hydraulic process, using volcanic ash (pozzolana) with added lime. World production is about 4.4 billion tonnes per year (2021 estimate), about half of it in China. Cement production is responsible for nearly 8% (2018) of global CO₂ emissions, although hydrated products such as concrete gradually reabsorb approximately 30% of the initial emissions through carbonation.

Designated place where the remains of many dead people are [[Burial|buried]] or otherwise entombed, also called a burial ground, gravesite or memorial park. The word derives from the Greek for "sleeping place" and was originally applied to the Roman catacombs. Remains may be interred in a grave, a tomb, a mausoleum, a columbarium or a niche. In Western cultures, [[Funeral|funeral]] ceremonies are often held at cemeteries, though rites differ by culture and religion, and modern cemeteries often include crematoria. Strictly, a graveyard is a burial ground within a churchyard. Modern cemeteries developed in the 18th and 19th centuries amid urbanization and concern over disease in overcrowded churchyards; landscaped "garden" cemeteries such as Mount Auburn in [[Boston|Boston]] in 1831 were designed as parks.

Turkish-American political commentator and activist, co-creator of the progressive news and commentary program *The Young Turks*, launched in 2002. He founded the political action committees Wolf-PAC, Justice Democrats and Rebellion PAC. He ran unsuccessfully as a Democrat for California's 25th congressional district in 2020. In 2023 he announced a campaign for the 2024 Democratic presidential primaries, with the stated aim of pressuring then-president Joe Biden to withdraw, and suspended it in March 2024. His past comments about women, minorities and other groups drew controversy, and he later apologized for and retracted them.

Natural pit or [[Sinkhole|sinkhole]] that forms when [[Limestone|limestone]] bedrock collapses to expose [[Groundwater|groundwater]]. The term originated on the [[Yucatán Peninsula|Yucatán Peninsula]] of Mexico, where the ancient Maya used cenotes as water supplies and occasionally for sacrificial offerings. Researchers now apply it to similar [[Karst|karst]] features in Cuba, Australia, Europe and the United States.

Current geological era of Earth's history, covering the last 66 million years and the most recent of three eras of the [[Phanerozoic|Phanerozoic]] Eon. Its name means "new life," and the era is characterized by the dominance of [[Mammal|mammals]], insects, birds and flowering plants. It began with the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]], which killed many species, including the non-avian [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]], and which most experts attribute to the Chicxulub impactor. Because mammals dominated the land in both hemispheres, the era is often called the Age of Mammals. Mammals and birds diversified greatly after the extinctions, and the continents moved into their present positions. Early Cenozoic climates were warmer than today, particularly during the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, but the Eocene to Oligocene transition and the Quaternary glaciation cooled and dried the Earth. The era is divided into the [[Paleogene|Paleogene]], [[Neogene|Neogene]] and [[Quaternary|Quaternary]] periods.

Suppression of [[Speech|speech]], public communication or other information on the grounds that it is considered objectionable, harmful, sensitive or "inconvenient." Censorship may be carried out by governments or private institutions, and creators may censor their own works, which is called self-censorship. It applies to books, music, films, the press, broadcasting and the [[Internet|Internet]]. Stated justifications include [[National security|national security]], control of obscenity, [[Pornography|pornography]] and hate speech, protection of children, promotion or restriction of political or religious views, and prevention of slander and libel. Rules differ between legal jurisdictions and private organizations. Examples include the 1933 book burnings in Nazi Germany and state control of publishing in the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]].

Procedure of systematically acquiring, recording and calculating information about the members of a population, usually presented as statistics. The word comes from the [[Latin|Latin]] *censere*, "to assess." Most censuses are national population and housing counts, though others cover agriculture, businesses and traffic. The [[United Nations|United Nations]] recommends population censuses at least every ten years and defines their essential features as individual enumeration, universality within a defined territory, simultaneity and defined periodicity. In the [[Roman Republic|Roman Republic]], the census listed all adult males fit for military service. Modern censuses are essential for international comparisons of statistics. The United States has held a decennial census since 1790, as required by its Constitution to apportion representation and direct taxes.

Creature from [[Greek mythology|Greek mythology]] with the upper body of a human and the lower body and legs of a [[Horse|horse]]. Centaurs were said to live in the mountains of Thessaly and were often portrayed as wild as untamed horses. In the Centauromachy, a legendary battle with the Lapiths, a human tribe of Thessaly, centaurs who attacked the guests at a wedding feast were driven out. Chiron, an exception, was a wise teacher of heroes including Achilles and Heracles. Centaurs also appear in [[Roman mythology|Roman mythology]] and the medieval bestiary, and remain a staple of modern fantastic literature.

Bright [[Constellation|constellation]] in the southern sky, one of the largest, and among the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer [[Ptolemy|Ptolemy]]. It remains one of the 88 modern constellations. In Greek mythology it represents a [[Centaur|centaur]], a creature that is half human and half horse. Notable stars include [[Alpha Centauri|Alpha Centauri]], the nearest star system to the [[Solar System|Solar System]], its neighbor in the sky Beta Centauri, and HR 5171, one of the largest stars yet discovered. The constellation also contains [[Omega Centauri|Omega Centauri]], the brightest globular cluster visible from Earth and the largest identified in the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]], possibly a remnant of a [[Dwarf galaxy|dwarf galaxy]].

Radio galaxy in the southern constellation [[Centaurus|Centaurus]], also known as NGC 5128. Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it in 1826 from Parramatta, New South Wales. It is the closest radio galaxy to Earth and the fifth-brightest galaxy in the sky, though its distance (11–13 million light-years) and Hubble type, lenticular or giant elliptical, are debated. Its central [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]], with a mass of 55 million solar masses, ejects a relativistic jet that produces X-ray and radio emissions. Radio observations show the inner jet moving at about half the speed of light, and the radio jets extend more than a million light-years. The galaxy is also one of the nearest large starburst galaxies, and a galactic collision is suspected of triggering an intense burst of [[Star formation|star formation]].

Predatory [[Arthropod|arthropod]] of the class Chilopoda, a group in the subphylum Myriapoda that includes [[Millipede|millipedes]]. Centipedes have elongated, segmented bodies with one pair of legs per segment. Despite the name, no species has exactly 100 legs; they have an odd number of leg pairs, ranging from 15 to 191. All are [[Venom|venomous]], injecting venom through pincer-like forcipules, which are modified front legs rather than fangs. Predominantly generalist carnivores, they live in habitats from [[Tropical rainforest|tropical rainforests]] to [[Desert|deserts]]. Lacking the waxy [[Cuticle|cuticle]] of [[Insect|insects]] and [[Arachnid|arachnids]], they need moist microhabitats and avoid direct sunlight, staying under cover or active at night.

Subregion of the African continent, defined differently by different bodies. The United Nations uses the term Middle Africa for nine countries: [[Angola|Angola]], [[Cameroon|Cameroon]], the [[Central African Republic|Central African Republic]], [[Chad|Chad]], the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Democratic Republic of the Congo]], [[Equatorial Guinea|Equatorial Guinea]], [[Gabon|Gabon]], the Republic of the Congo, and São Tomé and Príncipe. Its UN office also covers Burundi and Rwanda, which the geoscheme places in [[East Africa|East Africa]]. Six of these countries also belong to the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa and share the Central African CFA franc. The African Development Bank defines the region as seven countries. The Congo Basin, the world's second-largest river basin and a major tropical rainforest system, dominates the region's environment.

Landlocked country in [[Central Africa|Central Africa]] (pop., 2024: 5,357,744). It is bordered by [[Chad|Chad]], [[Sudan|Sudan]], [[South Sudan|South Sudan]], the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo and [[Cameroon|Cameroon]], and covers about 620,000 sq km. Its capital and largest city is [[Bangui|Bangui]], on the southern border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The territory was a French colony known as Ubangi-Shari before independence in 1960. Autocratic rulers followed, including Jean-Bédel Bokassa, who renamed the country the Central African Empire and ruled as monarch from 1976 to 1979. The Central African Bush War began in 2004, and civil war resumed in 2012 despite peace treaties in 2007 and 2011. Sango is the national language and, with French, co-official. Most of the land is [[Savanna|Sudano-Guinean savanna]], with equatorial forest in the south.

Region of Asia comprising Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and most of Kazakhstan. Its arid [[Steppe|steppes]], mountain ranges such as the [[Tian Shan|Tian Shan]], and deserts including the Karakum and Kyzylkum supported nomadic pastoralism alongside irrigated agriculture in river valleys. Iranian peoples such as the [[Bactria|Bactrians]], [[Sogdia|Sogdians]] and Scythians inhabited the region predominantly before and in the early Islamic era. Turkic migration made it the homeland of the Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Turkmens, [[Uyghurs|Uyghurs]] and Uzbeks, and Turkic languages largely replaced Iranian ones, except in Tajikistan. The [[Silk Road|Silk Road]] trade routes crossed the region. From the mid-19th century until near the end of the 20th century, Central Asia was part of the [[Russian Empire|Russian Empire]] and then the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]]. The five countries became independent after the Soviet dissolution in 1991.

Geographical region of Europe lying between Eastern, Southern, Western and Northern Europe, marked by cultural diversity and some shared history. It is defined in different ways but often includes Austria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and Switzerland. The [[Habsburg monarchy|Habsburg monarchy]] ruled much of the region in the 18th century. After World War II the [[Iron Curtain|Iron Curtain]] divided Europe into the Western and [[Eastern Bloc|Eastern Blocs]], and the region's countries have often been classed as either Eastern or Western Europe.

Civilian foreign intelligence service of the U.S. federal government, which collects and analyzes intelligence and conducts covert operations. Established in 1947 under the National Security Act, it is headquartered in Langley, Virginia. Unlike the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|Federal Bureau of Investigation]], it has no law enforcement function and focuses on intelligence gathered overseas. It coordinates human intelligence across the U.S. Intelligence Community. Its covert activities, which have included involvement in regime changes, have been the subject of criticism.

Urban park in [[Manhattan|Manhattan]], [[New York City|New York City]], between the Upper West Side and Upper East Side neighborhoods. It was the first landscaped park in the United States. At 843 acres (341 ha), it is the sixth-largest park in the city and the most visited urban park in the United States, with an estimated 42 million visitors annually as of 2016. The park is owned by the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation, but since 1998 the non-profit Central Park Conservancy has managed it under a public–private partnership. [[Frederick Law Olmsted|Frederick Law Olmsted]] and Calvert Vaux won an 1858 design competition with their "Greensward Plan." Construction began in 1857, and existing settlements, including Seneca Village, were seized by eminent domain and razed. The park was completed in 1876, and Robert Moses began a clean-up program in the 1930s after a period of decline.
